controls.name: HTTPS transport for Export API
controls.description: The Export API is exposed as a public HTTPS service, providing TLS encryption in transit for export requests, download links, and export file transfers.
limitations: HTTPS prevents passive network eavesdropping on export requests, download links, and file contents but does not itself enforce tenant isolation or bind a download link to the original requester.

controls.name: Storage lifecycle policy for export files
controls.description: Completed export files written to the managed object store are subject to a storage lifecycle policy that retains them for 30 days and then expires them, allowing operators to retrieve recent exports within that window.
limitations: The lifecycle policy bounds retention to 30 days but does not guarantee immediate deletion after customer download, and documentation does not state whether this behaviour is visible to or aligned with what customers are told.

controls.name: Customer authentication for export requests and downloads
controls.description: The Customer actor is described as the authenticated requester and downloader of exports, indicating that export operations require an authenticated customer identity.
limitations: Documentation does not describe how customer authentication is implemented, which identity provider is used, or whether authentication is enforced at the point where a download link is redeemed.

mappings.applicability_reason: This threat involves only the customer-facing Export API and the managed object store used for export files (evd-001, evd-002, evd-003). No administrative or operator interface is involved in the described attack path, so the requirement’s applicable conditions about a privileged administrative interface and operator actions on customer data do not bear on this threat scenario.

The components and data flows in this threat describe a traditional export service (Export API, Export worker, managed object store) with no model invocation or AI processing (evd-001, evd-002, evd-003). No content is passed to a model, so the requirement about treating untrusted model input does not bear on this threat.

The export service simply assembles and serves customer data exports; there is no description of model output being generated or published externally (evd-001, evd-002, evd-003). Therefore the conditions for model output publication do not apply to this threat.

The architecture describes customer data being assembled into exports and stored in a managed object store (evd-001, evd-003, evd-006), but there is no use of an external model provider for analysis. The requirement about minimizing data sent to an external model provider does not bear on this export-link threat.

No model output is rendered into a user interface or markup in the described export flow; the system assembles and serves export files of existing customer records (evd-001, evd-003). The requirement about encoding model output for rendering does not bear on unauthorized export downloads.

The threat concerns misuse of an export download link once a customer is authenticated, not how user authentication is delegated or documented. The architecture notes that the Customer is authenticated (evd-004) but provides no indication of delegated authentication to an external identity provider, and whether authentication is delegated or local does not affect the described cross-tenant download via a leaked link.

The threat actor is a standard customer requesting and downloading exports over the public HTTPS Export API (evd-001, evd-002, evd-004). No privileged or administrative interface is used, so the requirement about establishing responsibility for multi-factor authentication on administrative or privileged access does not bear on this scenario.

The export service produces per-customer exports and serves multiple customers ("customers on request", evd-001). Exports containing a customer’s records are written to a shared managed object store (evd-003, evd-006), and the threat explicitly concerns one customer obtaining another customer’s export via a leaked or guessed link. This is a tenant-isolation and authorization problem, matching the requirement that every request be constrained to the correct tenant using server-side state.
assumptions: Assumed that the plural "customers" in evd-001 implies the service is multi-tenant, serving more than one customer organization.
Assumed that exports written to the managed object store for different customers share that storage system (evd-003, evd-006).

mappings.applicability_reason: The threat involves direct exports of this system’s own customer records via the Export API and managed object store (evd-001, evd-002, evd-003). There is no described delegated access to an external platform on behalf of customers, so the requirement about limiting integration privileges for external delegated access does not bear on this scenario.

The described attack path concerns runtime behaviour of the Export API, export files, and the managed object store (evd-001, evd-002, evd-003, evd-006). It does not involve the build or deployment pipeline or third-party components entering the build, so the requirement about trusting the deployment path and dependencies does not bear on this threat.

Export files contain a customer’s records for a requested date range (evd-001, evd-003), which are treated as confidential in the threat description, and are written to a managed object store (evd-003, evd-006). These exports are requested and downloaded over a public HTTPS service that crosses an untrusted network boundary (evd-002, df-001). Therefore the conditions that sensitive data is stored and transmitted across a network boundary are met.
mappings.suppressed_conclusion: Do not conclude that encryption at rest or its documentation is absent for the managed object store simply because the architecture and operations documents do not describe it.
mappings.suppressed_by: req-DATA-001 common false positive: "absent encryption detail for a managed service that encrypts by default" indicates missing detail is not evidence that encryption at rest is absent.
assumptions: Assumed that customer records contained in exports are confidential data for the purposes of encryption requirements.
Assumed that the managed object store is a distinct storage system whose encryption behaviour must be established rather than inferred.

mappings.applicability_reason: Assembled export files are described as temporary working data written to a managed object store (evd-003), and the operations guide specifies a storage lifecycle policy that retains completed export files for 30 days and then expires them (evd-006). The system therefore retains by-product customer data after processing, so the requirement about defining and enforcing a retention period applies.
assumptions: Assumed that export files in the managed object store are considered sensitive working copies of customer data rather than public data.

mappings.applicability_reason: Exports for different customers are assembled from their records and written to a single managed object store as export objects (evd-003, evd-006), so artifacts belonging to multiple customers share a storage system. The threat is specifically that a malicious customer could use a leaked or guessed download link to retrieve another customer’s export from this shared store, so the requirement to document how stored artifacts are separated and how that separation is enforced on access directly bears on this threat.
assumptions: Assumed that exports for more than one customer are stored in the same managed object store based on the shared storage description in evd-003 and evd-006.

mappings.applicability_reason: The threat concerns unauthorized access to an existing export file via a leaked or guessed download link, not the ability to remove all customer data across primary and derived stores on request. While deletion capabilities affect long-term retention of customer data, they do not prevent the described cross-tenant download once an export exists and a link has leaked.

The attack path involves a customer using a download link to retrieve an export file from the Export API or backing store (evd-001, evd-002, evd-003). Although logs may exist, leakage of sensitive data through logs is not part of this threat, and controlling log content would not prevent or materially change the unauthorized download described.

The threat involves actions taken by ordinary customers via the Export API, not privileged operators performing administrative actions on customer data or security configuration (evd-001, evd-004). Therefore the requirement to record security-relevant administrative actions does not bear on this specific threat.

Completed exports containing multiple customers’ data over time are written to a managed object store (evd-003, evd-006), which functions as an internal data store holding tenant-scoped artifacts. The Export API is a public HTTPS interface (evd-002), and the threat acknowledges that either the Export API or the storage layer might serve the export via the download link. This matches the requirement’s focus on ensuring that internal stores holding multi-tenant data are reachable only from the workloads that use them, not broadly from untrusted networks.
assumptions: Assumed that the managed object store is intended as an internal storage component and not as a general public interface, based on its description as a managed object store backing the export service (evd-003, evd-006).

mappings.applicability_reason: The threat involves per-export download links that may function as bearer tokens for specific export files, but there is no described long-lived credential or signing key whose compromise would itself enable access to customer resources. The requirement about storing long-lived signing keys and provider credentials in a managed secret store applies to system credentials for external platforms, which are not part of this attack path.

The scenario describes customers requesting and downloading exports via the Export API using download links (evd-001, evd-002, evd-003). It does not describe the system accessing customer resources on an external platform using tokens or installation-scoped credentials, so the requirement about using short-lived credentials for external customer resources does not bear on this threat.

While a managed object store is used, the threat concerns one customer obtaining another customer’s export through a leaked or guessed link within this service’s architecture (evd-001, evd-003, evd-006). It does not involve an external processor making independent use of customer data, nor do provider retention and usage terms affect whether cross-tenant exports can be downloaded, so this requirement does not bear on the threat.

The export process is initiated by authenticated customer requests over HTTPS (evd-001, evd-002, evd-004). There is no described metered external service being consumed per unit of work or unbounded externally triggered processing, so the requirement about bounding work triggered by external events does not bear on this threat.

The system exposes a public HTTPS Export API that customers call directly to request and download exports (evd-001, evd-002). There is no inbound webhook or event endpoint receiving events from an external platform, so the requirement about verifying inbound event authenticity does not bear on this threat.

No webhook or externally delivered event mechanism is described; export processing is initiated by direct customer requests to the Export API (evd-001, evd-002). Therefore the requirement about preventing or making harmless the replay of inbound events does not apply to this threat.

documentation_gaps.title: Authorization and binding model for export download links is undocumented
documentation_gaps.description: The documentation describes that the Export API returns a download link when an export is ready (evd-002) and that the Customer is the authenticated requester and downloader of an export (evd-004), but it does not state how a download link is authorized when used. In particular, it is unclear whether the link is bound to the authenticated customer identity or tenant, whether additional authorization checks are performed when the link is redeemed, and whether possession of the URL alone is sufficient to download the export. This prevents determining whether a leaked or guessed link would allow cross-tenant access as described in threat thr-001.
documentation_gaps.importance: Without clarity on how export download links are bound to the requesting customer and authorized at use time, it is impossible to assess whether tenant-aware authorization (req-AUTHZ-001) is actually enforced for export downloads or whether the link functions as an unscoped bearer token, which is central to this threat.
requested_evidence: Architecture or design documentation describing the authorization checks performed when a download link is used, including how the tenant/customer context is derived and enforced.
A description of whether download links are single-use or time-limited, and how their validity is enforced.
Clarification on whether the download link targets the Export API, the managed object store directly (for example via a presigned URL), or both, and how authorization differs between these paths.

documentation_gaps.title: Tenant separation and access control for export files in the managed object store are undocumented
documentation_gaps.description: Exports containing a customer’s records are written to a managed object store and retained under a lifecycle policy (evd-003, evd-006). However, the documentation does not describe how export objects are named or organized by tenant, what access policies apply to the store, or how reads of stored exports are authorized. This leaves it unclear whether one customer could reach another customer’s export in the store, especially when using a leaked or guessed download link as in threat thr-001.
documentation_gaps.importance: Understanding how export artifacts are separated and how access to them is enforced is necessary to evaluate req-DATA-003 and req-NET-001 in the context of cross-tenant export downloads. Without this, the strength of the tenant boundary around stored exports cannot be assessed.
requested_evidence: Documentation of the storage layout for export objects, including any per-tenant prefixes, buckets, or keys.
A description of the access policies on the managed object store (for example, which principals can read export objects and whether public or presigned access is allowed).
An explanation of how the application or storage layer enforces that only the owning customer or tenant can access a given export object.

documentation_gaps.title: Export retention behaviour and customer-facing expectations are unclear
documentation_gaps.description: The architecture overview describes the export file as temporary working data that is deleted immediately once the customer has downloaded it (evd-003), while the operations guide describes a storage lifecycle policy that retains completed export files for 30 days and allows operators to retrieve recent exports within that window (evd-006). It is not clear which behaviour is authoritative, how these two descriptions relate, or what customers are told about export retention.
documentation_gaps.importance: The actual retention period for export files affects how long a leaked or guessed download link might remain usable and whether the retention enforced in storage matches what customers are told, both of which are relevant to req-DATA-002 and the impact of threat thr-001.
requested_evidence: Clarification of the intended retention behaviour for export files, including whether they are deleted immediately after successful download or retained for a configured period (such as 30 days).
An indication of which documentation (if any) is customer-facing for export retention, and confirmation that it matches the implemented lifecycle behaviour.
Reference to the actual storage lifecycle configuration used for the managed object store holding export files.

documentation_gaps.title: Encryption at rest for export files in the managed object store is not documented
documentation_gaps.description: Export files containing customer records are written to a managed object store and retained for up to 30 days (evd-003, evd-006). The documentation does not state whether these objects are encrypted at rest, whether encryption is inherited from the managed object store provider, or how keys are managed. This prevents verifying the at-rest portion of req-DATA-001 for the export artifacts central to this threat.
documentation_gaps.importance: If export files are not encrypted at rest, compromise of the storage or backups could expose full export datasets beyond access via the download link, increasing the impact of threat thr-001. Even if encryption is inherited from the platform, documenting this and naming the provider is required to fully satisfy req-DATA-001.
requested_evidence: Documentation stating whether the managed object store encrypts export objects at rest and, if so, whether this is inherited from the platform or configured by the application team.
Details of the key management approach (for example, use of a cloud key management service or provider-managed keys).
References to the managed object store or platform configuration demonstrating encryption-at-rest settings.
